title: Index arithmetic (interval length, midpoint, slice, wrap)
description: The +1 / -1 / midpoint / modulo idioms behind sliding windows, binary search, fixed-length slices, and circular indexing — the arithmetic you reach for before the algorithm.

notes: Inclusive length needs +1 because subtraction undercounts the left endpoint.
`(lo + hi) >> 1` is the idiomatic floor-divide for midpoint — interviewers expect it over `Math.floor((lo+hi)/2)`.
`slice(start, start + n)` gives exactly n items because slice's end is EXCLUSIVE — a frequent off-by-one source.
JS `%` keeps the sign of the dividend, so wrapping a negative index needs `((i % n) + n) % n`, not just `i % n`.

questions.q: How many elements are between indices l=2 and r=6, INCLUSIVE of both endpoints?
questions.explain: Inclusive length is r - l + 1. The +1 counts the left endpoint that the subtraction would otherwise drop.

questions.q: Binary search: what is the midpoint of lo=3 and hi=10 using `(lo + hi) >> 1`?
questions.explain: (3 + 10) >> 1 = 13 >> 1 = 6. Right-shift by 1 is integer divide by 2 (floor).

questions.q: You want a sub-array of exactly 4 elements starting at index 2. Which call?
questions.explain: slice's 2nd arg is EXCLUSIVE, so end = start + n gives exactly n items. arr.slice(2, 4) returns only 2 elements.

questions.q: What does `arr[-1]` return in JavaScript when arr = [10, 20, 30]?
options: undefined — JS arrays don't support negative bracket indices
questions.explain: JS array bracket access with a negative index is just a missing property lookup → undefined. Use `arr.at(-1)` for the Python-style behavior.

exercises.prompt: Count elements between l=2 and r=7 INCLUSIVE — fill in the arithmetic.
Take exactly 3 elements from index 1 using slice — fill in the second arg.

blanks.hint: end is exclusive — add n to start

exercises.prompt: Wrap a possibly-negative index into a circular array — fill in the modulo dance.

blanks.hint: second modulo by n folds the result back into [0, n)

L3.prompt: Write `maxWindowSum(arr, k)` that returns the maximum sum over any sliding window of size k, using r - l + 1 = k as the window-length invariant. Log `maxWindowSum([2, 1, 5, 1, 3, 2], 3)`.
hints: Seed `sum` with the first k elements, then slide.
When the right pointer advances to r, the element leaving the window is arr[r - k] (because window length k = r - l + 1 means l = r - k + 1).
